query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA, the supersaturated solid‐solution state supports Mg segregation that, upon thermal exposure, rapidly transforms into fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates (akin to MgZn2-type phases seen in similar Al-containing HEAs). These precipitates modify the grain boundary and surface chemistry, enhancing high-temperature oxidation resistance (by promoting formation of a protective Mg-rich oxide scale) while potentially increasing localized galvanic effects and hence corrosion susceptibility relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, non-equilibrium lightweight HEA with a dominant supersaturated solid solution in which Mg is largely dissolved with minor local segregation.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging (or high-temperature exposure) under oxidizing conditions.
generation.conditions: Aging under isothermal conditions (e.g., 300–500 °C in air) for a defined period, with compositions restricted to densities below 6 g/cm³ and containing Mg alongside other elements (e.g., Al, Cu, Zn, Gd).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates concentrated at grain boundaries and surfaces.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation drives Mg segregation and precipitate formation from the initial supersaturated state; the precipitates in turn alter local chemical potentials and microstructure. The resulting Mg-rich oxide layers on the surface improve oxidation resistance, but their chemical heterogeneity may also enhance localized corrosion through galvanic interactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, thermally aged samples will show a more stable and protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, yet exhibit increased sensitivity to localized (intergranular) corrosion in corrosive environments due to the precipitate-induced chemical inhomogeneity.
generation.baseline: The initially cast alloy state with a uniform, metastable solid solution and minimal intermetallic formation.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected only in lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ and sufficient Mg content to trigger precipitate formation; variations in processing histories or alloying elements that do not permit Mg segregation may not follow the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise transformation temperatures, precipitate sizes/distributions, and quantitative extent of the oxidation and corrosion property changes are uncertain due to the complex interplay of multicomponent alloy chemistry and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the targeted Mg-containing lightweight HEA: one set remains in the as-cast state (baseline), and the other is subjected to controlled thermal aging under oxidizing conditions (e.g., 300–500 °C for a fixed duration). Following treatment, perform high-temperature oxidation tests (such as thermogravimetric analysis to assess oxide scale development) and electrochemical corrosion testing (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in a chloride electrolyte). Analyze microstructural changes using SEM/EDS and XRD to verify the presence or absence of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
measurements: Weight gain during high-temperature oxidation (to assess oxide scale formation)
Electrochemical corrosion current densities and potentials
Microstructural and phase identification (SEM, EDS, XRD) to detect precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not result in the formation of detectable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates and/or there is no statistically significant improvement in high-temperature oxidation resistance or change in corrosion behavior (relative to the as-cast baseline), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Effect of Al Content and Local Chemical Order on the Stacking Fault Energy in Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al High-Entropy Alloys Based on First Principles

Abstract: AbstractAs a promising candidate for next-generation aviation structural materials, lightweight refractory high entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit high strength, low density, and excellent high-temperature performance. In this study, we investigated the influence of local chemical ordering on the properties of Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al HEAs using Monte Carlo (MC) simulations based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations. We established that the chemical short-range ordering (SRO) in Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al HEAs increases with the Al content, resulting in a gradual increase in stacking fault energy (SFE). Al-Ti-Containing Lightweight High-Entropy Alloys for Intermediate Temperature Applications

Abstract: AbstractIn this study, new high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain lightweight elements, namely Al and Ti, have been designed for intermediate temperature applications. Cr, Mo, and V were selected as the elements for the Al-Ti-containing HEAs by elemental screening using their binary phase diagrams. AlCrMoTi and AlCrMoTiV HEAs are confirmed as solid solutions with minor ordered B2 phases and have superb specific hardness when compared to that of commercial alloys. The present work demonstrates the desirable possibility for substitution of traditional materials that are applied at intermediate temperature to Al-Ti-containing lightweight HEAs.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, alloys design, lightweight alloys

Conclusions: In summary, HEAs which contained Al and Ti were designed based on their binary phase diagrams. This approach is powerful for screening candidate elements for novel HEAs. The Effect of Scandium Ternary Intergrain Precipitates in Al-Containing High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: We investigate the effect of alloying with scandium on microstructure, high-temperature phase stability, electron transport, and mechanical properties of the Al2CoCrFeNi, Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi, and AlCoCrCu0.5FeNi high-entropy alloys. Out of the three model alloys, Al2CoCrFeNi adopts a disordered CsCl structure type. Both of the six-component alloys contain a mixture of body-centered cubic (bcc) and face centered cubic (fcc) phases. The comparison between in situ high-temperature powder diffraction data and ex situ data from heat-treated samples highlights the presence of a reversible bcc to fcc transition. The precipitation of a MgZn2-type intermetallic phase along grain boundaries following scandium addition affects all systems differently, but especially enhances the properties of Al2CoCrFeNi. It causes grain refinement; hardness and electrical conductivity increases (up to 20% and 14% respectively) and affects the CsCl-type → fcc equilibrium by moving the transformation to sensibly higher temperatures. The maximum dimensionless thermoelectric figure of merit (ZT) of 0.014 is reached
